citeinfo.title: Digital elevation model of Mount St. Helens, Washington and vicinity prior to the 1980 eruption
citeinfo.othercit: Suggested citation: Bard, J.A. and Phillips-Netherton, R. 2024, Digital elevation model of Mount St. Helens, Washington and vicinity prior to the 1980 eruption: U.S. Geological Survey data release, https://doi.org/10.5066/P91W7C1L

descript.abstract: On May 18, 1980, Mount St. Helens, Washington, exploded in a spectacular and devastating eruption that resulted in previously unimaginable events that drastically altered the mountain and the surrounding area. One unprecedented event was the collapse of the summit and north flank of the volcano forming a huge landslide known as the ‘debris avalanche’ with a total volume of about 2.5 km3 (3.3 billion cubic yards). The debris avalanche swept around and up ridges to the north, but most of it turned westward as far as 23 km (14 mi) down the valley of the North Fork Toutle River and formed a hummocky deposit. This had a profound effect on the topography of the area, including transforming the summit cone of the volcano into an amphitheater-shaped crater, in places, burying the valley north of the volcano under hundreds of feet of debris, and filling the Spirit Lake basin raising the surface elevation 64 m (210 ft). This release consists of a 10-meter resolution digital elevation model, covering an area of 196.45 sq km, and hillshade map of the summit and valley north of the volcano circa 1952 surface derived from contour lines digitized from historic topographic maps. These data represent the paleo topography of Mt St. Helens and vicinity that were most significantly altered by the 1980 eruption and debris avalanche.
descript.purpose: These data, a raster digital elevation model derived historic topographic maps of Mount St. Helens and the adjacent vicinity, contribute to the study of volcanic landforms and landscape modification resulting from volcanic eruptions.
descript.supplinf: The DEM in this release is well fit to the source maps and therefore provides an adequate representation of the topography surface prior to the 1980 eruption. Users of these data must be aware of the inherent limitations of source maps and of the methods used to derive these data. Although the digital form of these data removes the constraint imposed by the scale of a paper maps (1:62,500), the detail and accuracy of these data cannot be greater than that of the source maps. Prior to the 1980 eruption, the most current topographic maps of the area were published in the 1950s at a scale of 1:62,500 with contours derived photogrammetrically from aerial photographs captured in 1952. At this time, dense stands of mature conifer forests encircled the volcano, potentially obscuring view of the bare ground in some places within the extent of the maps that comprise this release. The method for creating the DEM uses averaging to reduce 'stair-step' artifacts in areas with shallow slopes or low relief, which commonly occur with interpolation methods taking contour lines as inputs. The resulting DEM is smoother than USGS DEMs of similar resolution and subtle topographic features are not present in many areas and spot elevations specified in the source maps may not be exatly reproduced within this DEM.

attracc.attraccr: Absolute accuracy assessment of these data with respect to the ground surface is not possible in areas that were drastically altered by the 1980 eruption. Therefore, accuracy of these data was assessed relative to the source topographic maps. Relative vertical accuracy was assessed by sampling the DEM at 55,304 points along the digitized contour lines and taking the differences between the expected values (contour elevations) and measured values (DEM elevations). Relative horizontal accuracy was assessed by comparing the locations these points to contours lines derived from the DEM of the same elevations. The absolute horizontal accuracy standard for USGS topographic maps requires that the positions of 90 percent of all points tested must be accurate within 1/50th of an inch (0.05 centimeters) on the map. For 1:62,500 the source maps, 1/50th of an inch on the map equates to 31.76 m (104.16 ft) on the ground. The absolute vertical accuracy standard for USGS topographic maps require that the elevation of 90 percent of all points tested must be correct within half of the contour interval. Contour interval of the source maps is 80 ft (24.384 m). The measured relative horizontal and relative vertical error of the DEM are within the envelope of error of the absolute accuracy standards required for a 1:62,500 scale USGS topographic map.

procstep.procdesc: Digitize topographic maps using ArcGIS Pro to create vectors datasets (a) of 80 ft interval elevation contour lines [Contours_80], (b) stream lines, (c) lake polygons, and (d) elevation points, e.g., mountain peaks. Source maps are scanned paper 1:62,500 USGS topographic maps, and in the summit area, scanned stable mylar bases. Therefore, in the summit region, lines are considered accurate but may not exactly match the scanned paper maps. The scanned paper maps were hand digitized by tracing the contours, lakes, streams, and point elevations. In the summit region, the scanned mylar base was edited to remove all pixels that did not represent contour lines (e.g. text and glacial extents). The Thin tool was used to prepare the image for creating vector lines using the Raster to Polyline tool. Finally, all elevation attributes were added to the contour lines and the topology was verified.

Interpolate a DEM [DEM_B] using the Borgefors distance method described in the ILWIS 3.0 User’s Guide, 2001 (see Cross Reference for citation). Following recommendations in the User's Guide, small enclosed contours were created to supplement the digitized contours on hilltops to improve the interpolation in these areas (without these additional contours hilltops may be artificially flattened).
Applying a smoothing mean function (ArcGIS Pro Focal Statistics tool, 3x3 window) to DEM_B to create DEM_S.

From DEM_S, generate 2 ft interval contour lines [Contours_2ft] using ArcGIS Pro Contour function. The Contour tool's documentation recommends applying a smoothing function to prepare a DEM for contouring.

Interpolate 8 DEMs [DEM_1-DEM_8] using the ArcGIS Pro Topo to Raster tool with default parameters. Inputs are elevation contours, stream lines, lake polygons, and elevation points. All DEMs uses the same stream, lake, and elevation points, but the elevation contours are varied such that DEM_1 uses Contours_80 supplemented with contours at 16 ft intervals from Contours_2ft, DEM_2 uses a subset Contours_2ft where each contour values is 2 ft greater than the contours used to produce DEM_1, and this pattern is repeated for DEM_3-DEM_8. For example: If the contours used to create DEM_1 are Elevation (ft) = (0, 16, 32, 48, 64, 80), the contours used to create DEM_2 are Elevation (ft) = (2, 18, 34, 50, 66, 82), the contours used to create DEM_3 are Elevation (ft) = (4, 20, 36, 52, 68, 84)…, the contours used to create DEM_8 are Elevation (ft) = (14, 30, 46, 62, 78, 94)
Use ArcGIS Raster Calculator to calculate the arithmetic mean of DEM_1-DEM_8 to create DEM_Mean.

Use ArcGIS Pro Extract by Mask tool to subset DEM_Mean to create DEM_Mask. The mask is a polygon equal to the extent of the original contour lines, buffered -100 m inward from the edge to reduce erroneous values and edge effects due to the interpolation method used by the Topo to Raster tool.
Reproject DEM_Mask from North_American_1927_Polyconic to NAD83 UTM10 N to create the final DEM: msh_1952_dem_nad83_utm10.tif
